meta.purpose: Professional Communication Academy — communication built on finance situations, not generic English lessons.
meta.method: Fifteen minutes of speaking and fifteen minutes of writing every day, both recorded or filed. Fluency comes from repetition under mild pressure, not from reading about fluency.
meta.rule: Every exercise must produce an artefact: an audio file, a written piece or a marked-up draft.

levels.name: Foundational
levels.outcome: Speak in complete sentences for two minutes without long pauses; write a clear short email.

levels.name: Professional
levels.outcome: Explain a number and its cause in writing and in speech, with a clear recommendation.

levels.name: Influential
levels.outcome: Present to management, handle challenge, and hold a position with evidence.

levels.name: Career-ready
levels.outcome: Perform under interview conditions and represent your own work credibly.

areas.name: Spoken English
areas.outcome: Speak about finance topics in connected speech at a professional pace.
focus: Structuring a spoken answer in three points
Accent clarity rather than accent removal
drills: Speak for 90 seconds on 'the difference between profit and cash' without notes. Record and count filler words.
Read a paragraph of a financial newspaper aloud, then summarise it in 60 seconds.
Explain a ratio to a non-finance friend in under a minute, then check whether they understood.
Say five large numbers aloud correctly: ₹12,45,67,890; ₹4.72 crore; 18.5%; 2.75 times; ₹1.2 lakh per month.
areas.successTest: Two minutes of connected speech with fewer than five filler words and accurate number reading.

areas.name: Business English
areas.outcome: Write and speak in concise, unambiguous professional register.
focus: Register: internal vs client vs regulator
drills: Rewrite a 60-word email to 30 words without losing meaning.
Convert five passive sentences to active.
Rewrite three sentences that overstate certainty into appropriately hedged statements.
Identify and correct ten common usage errors in a provided paragraph.
areas.successTest: A 100-word professional note with no ambiguity, no redundancy and no overstatement.

areas.name: Professional and Finance Vocabulary
areas.outcome: Use the technical vocabulary of accounting and finance precisely, in context.
drills: Learn ten terms a week; for each, write a definition in your own words and one sentence using it in a work situation.
Distinguish five commonly confused pairs: provision/provision for doubtful debts; expense/expenditure; income/receipt; profit/contribution; cost/price.
Explain five acronyms you use daily without expanding them on autopilot: EBITDA, WACC, DSO, ITC, TDS.
areas.successTest: Explain 20 core terms to a layperson without using the term itself in the definition.

areas.name: Grammar and Accuracy
areas.outcome: Write without errors that undermine credibility.
drills: Edit a 200-word draft and mark every correction with a reason.
Write five conditional sentences describing scenario outcomes (if volume falls 10%...).
Format numbers consistently in a table: units, decimals, thousands separators, currency.
Rewrite ten sentences with misplaced modifiers.
areas.successTest: A 200-word piece with zero grammatical or formatting errors on review.

areas.name: Email Writing
areas.outcome: Write emails that get a decision or an action on the first attempt.
focus: Subject lines that state the ask
drills: Write an email asking a department head for an overdue explanation of a 22% cost overrun, without sounding accusatory.
Write a three-line email declining a supplier's price increase, with the reason and the next step.
Rewrite an email that buries the request in paragraph four.
Write an escalation email that states facts, impact and the specific decision required by a specific date.
areas.successTest: A recipient can state the ask and the deadline after reading only the subject line and first line.

areas.name: Report Writing
areas.outcome: Produce a report that a busy reader can act on in five minutes.
drills: Write a one-page variance report: what happened, why, what to do, by when, and who owns it.
Convert a five-page descriptive report into a two-page decision document.
Write an executive summary last for a report you have already drafted, then check it stands alone.
Write a limitations section for an analysis you produced this week.
areas.successTest: A reader who reads only the summary and recommendations can make the decision.

areas.name: Presentation Skills
areas.outcome: Present with structure and composure, and handle challenge.
drills: Deliver a three-minute presentation with one message, three supports and one ask.
Present the same content in 60 seconds, then in 20 seconds.
Take three challenge questions and answer each in under 30 seconds with evidence.
Present a number you are not confident about, and state the uncertainty honestly.
areas.successTest: Audience can repeat your main message after the presentation.

areas.name: Interview Communication
areas.outcome: Present your experience credibly under interview conditions.
focus: Explaining technical work to a non-technical interviewer
drills: Prepare six STAR stories covering a cost saving, a conflict, a failure, a deadline, an analysis that changed a decision, and a process improvement.
Answer 'tell me about yourself' in 90 seconds, ending with why this role.
Explain a model you built to someone with no finance background in two minutes.
Record answers to ten standard interview questions and review them against a rubric.
areas.successTest: Every claim is supported by a specific example with a measurable outcome.

areas.name: Group Discussions
areas.outcome: Contribute to a group discussion with structure, evidence and listening.
focus: Entering the discussion early with substance
Building on others rather than repeating
drills: Run a 10-minute mock GD on 'should companies prioritise cost reduction or revenue growth in a downturn?' and record it.
Practise three ways to enter a discussion without interrupting.
Write a 60-second summary of a discussion you observed, capturing both sides.
areas.successTest: You made three substantive contributions, built on at least two others, and did not dominate.

areas.name: Financial Presentations
areas.outcome: Present numbers so the story is understood before the detail.
focus: Explaining a bridge without losing the audience
drills: Narrate a five-bar waterfall bridge in 60 seconds, naming each driver.
Present a 12% revenue miss to a management team in three minutes, ending with a recovery plan.
Present a KPI dashboard and stop at three insights, not fifteen.
areas.successTest: The audience can name the driver of the result without reading the slide.

areas.name: Management Communication
areas.outcome: Communicate with senior stakeholders in the register they expect.
drills: Write a weekly update to a CFO in five bullets: performance, risk, decision needed, help needed, next week.
Convert a problem statement into a one-page options paper with a recommendation.
Write an email saying a deadline will slip, with the new date and the mitigation.
areas.successTest: A senior stakeholder gets the decision and the risk in the first ten seconds.

areas.name: Explaining Financial Results
areas.outcome: Explain a result to a non-finance audience without diluting accuracy.
focus: Translating accounting into cash and operations
Explaining a variance in operational terms
drills: Explain why profit rose while cash fell, to an operations manager, in 90 seconds.
Explain contribution margin to a sales head using their own product mix.
Answer 'why did cost per unit go up?' three times in a row, each time going one level deeper.
Explain a provision to a non-accountant without implying it is a cash payment.
areas.successTest: The listener can explain the result to someone else correctly.

rotation.speaking: Explain a concept: pick one term from this week's study and explain it aloud in 90 seconds.
rotation.writing: Write a 100-word email to a colleague summarising one thing you learned.

rotation.speaking: Number drill: read 10 figures aloud accurately, then use three in sentences.
rotation.writing: Write a 150-word paragraph explaining a variance with its cause.

rotation.speaking: Challenge drill: state a position on a finance question and defend it in 60 seconds.
rotation.writing: Rewrite a poorly written paragraph from a report or news article.

rotation.speaking: Teach-back: explain a calculation you did this week to an imaginary non-finance colleague.
rotation.writing: Write a three-bullet update to a manager: progress, risk, ask.

rotation.speaking: Interview drill: answer one behavioural question in STAR format, recorded.
rotation.writing: Write a one-page summary of the week's learning in professional prose.

rotation.speaking: Present a five-slide pack aloud in five minutes, recorded.
rotation.writing: Write a recommendation memo with options, analysis and a decision.

rotation.speaking: Listen to a finance podcast or lecture and summarise it aloud in two minutes.
rotation.writing: Edit the week's writing and log recurring errors in your knowledge base.

speakingPrompts: Why does a profitable company run out of cash?
Explain break-even to a shop owner.
Should a company buy or lease its delivery vehicles?
What is the difference between a provision and a reserve?
Why is depreciation added back in a cash flow statement?
How would you explain a 5% cost overrun to the department that caused it?
What does a current ratio of 0.8 tell you?
Why do two companies with the same profit have different share prices?
Explain the difference between gross margin and contribution.
Why is inventory a cash risk?
What is input tax credit and why does it matter to pricing?
How would you explain an adverse variance you cannot yet explain?
What is the difference between cost control and cost reduction?
Why is a budget not a forecast?
Explain the time value of money using an example from everyday life.
What are the risks of automating a reconciliation?
How would you describe your role as a management accountant to a school student?
Why should a CMA care about ethics?
What does a rising DSO indicate?
Explain why the cost of capital matters in an investment decision.
writingPrompts: Write a 120-word note explaining a 15% cost overrun to your manager, with a cause and a corrective action.
Draft an email requesting a missing invoice from a vendor, firm but courteous.
Write a 200-word executive summary of a variance analysis.
Write a one-paragraph recommendation on whether to discontinue a loss-making product.
Draft the body of a report section titled 'Basis of preparation and limitations'.
Write an email declining a request to book an expense in the wrong period, explaining the rule.
Write a 150-word explanation of the difference between absorption and marginal costing for a non-finance reader.
Draft a three-line update to a CFO on a delayed close.
Write a 250-word note explaining why profit and cash diverged this quarter.
Write a short memo proposing one cost optimisation with an estimated saving and a risk.

rubric.detail: Message is identifiable within the first two lines or twenty seconds.
Every number and claim is correct and traceable.
Register, technical level and length match the audience.
A clear ask, recommendation or next step.

selfCheck: Could a busy reader act on this immediately?
Is this the shortest version that is still complete?
Would I be comfortable if this were forwarded to a regulator?
